title: Three Pillars

post.author: u/desk_guard_temperance
post.title: I'm the night guard at an office building. My screen called last night the fastest night on record. Not one office was cleaned.

blocks.text: I'm Temperance, night guard at Larkhollow House, an office building with 40 offices. Tap your badge on a door's reader, and it asks a computer in the basement whether that badge may open that door. A computer that answers other machines' questions is a server; this one is the badge server. A tap that opens the door is a good entry.

Staff use the front door by my desk. Their badges are checked against the building's own list in 50 ms (ms is a thousandth of a second). The cleaners, from an agency called Sheencroft, may only use the side doors: two at the back, and a service door into each office. Their badges are checked against Sheencroft's register, its online list of who is working tonight, in about 600 ms.
My screen shows a dashboard: numbers, each drawn as a line across the night. A number measured again and again like this is a metric. Mine has two: taps a minute, and answer time.

The answer time is an average: every answer's time added up, divided by the number of answers. If it stays above 2 s for 5 minutes, a warning sounds, called an alert. We call it the speed alert. It has never gone off at night.
The badge server also keeps a log, its diary: one line per tap. Nobody reads it unless something has gone wrong.

In October, when Sheencroft took over the cleaning, Gwilherm, who looks after the badge system, linked it to their register on a free three-month trial. Nobody wrote down the end date. It ended at 00:00 last night. From then on the register answered every check at once: "payment required". Anything but yes keeps a door shut, so the side doors refused, in 40 ms.

The crew of eight starts at midnight, one cleaner a minute. Each was refused and tapped again, twice a minute. Here are lines from the first two minutes of the log; each shows the time, the door, the badge type, the register's answer (a dash if not asked) and how long the answer took:

00:00:10  side east  contractor  payment required  40 ms
00:00:40  side east  contractor  payment required  40 ms
00:01:02  front      staff       -                 50 ms
00:01:11  side west  contractor  payment required  40 ms
Zubaida, the crew lead, texted Sheencroft; nobody answered. At 00:40 the crew went home, after 584 refusals.

After midnight, taps a minute rose from the usual 1 to 17: a busy night. The answer time fell to 41 ms, because the average counts every answer, and a no was faster than any yes. No alert. At 05:00 the night report said 00:00 to 05:00 averaged 43 ms: the fastest night on record. Every answer before had taken 50 ms or more.
The fastest night on record was the night nobody got in.

At 07:00 the bins were full on every floor; not one office had been cleaned. Gwilherm pulled up a trace: one tap's path through every machine it touched, each step timed. Badge server, under 1 ms. Register, 40 ms, "payment required". Door, refused.
Every night before, the trial was running and almost every tap was a yes, so taps and speed were enough. What should Gwilherm change on my screen before the next shift?

blocks.label: badge_dashboard_night.png

diagram.aria: One hour from 23:50:00. The register answers normally until 00:00:00, then says payment required. The side doors refuse 584 taps, 40 ms each, from 00:00:10 to 00:39:47, and nobody taps them after the crew goes home at 00:40. The front door lets staff in all hour. The speed alert stays silent all hour, with the average between 41 and 50 ms.

blocks.caption: 23:50 to 00:50. At 00:00 the trial ends and the register says payment required to every check. The side doors refuse 584 taps from 00:00:10 to 00:39:47, each in 40 ms, and the crew goes home at 00:40. The speed alert never stirs: the average only falls.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Engineers call this observability: how well you can tell what a system is doing from what it reports about itself. Google's book on keeping big systems running names four signals worth watching on any service. Latency: how long answers take. Traffic: how many requests come in. Errors: how many fail; as a share of all requests, that is the error rate. Saturation: how full the machine is. Your screen shows two of the four. So, questions. How long did a no take, against a yes? What share of side-door taps opened a door last night? And who reads the log at 3 AM?

replies.author: u/desk_guard_temperance
replies.text: A no took 40 ms; a yes takes about 600. Of the 584 side-door taps, not one opened a door. The log had every line, and nobody read it until Gwilherm and I did, at half past seven.

comments.author: u/tighten_it_thorbjorn
comments.text: Your alert threshold is just too loose. Two seconds, for five minutes, for a badge check? A healthy check is well under a second. Tighten it to 1 s and you'd have caught it; something was plainly wrong with that register all night. An alert set so high that it never rings is decoration.

comments.author: u/cpu_watch_oluwaseyi
comments.text: Watch the machine, not the doors. A server's CPU is its processor, the chip that does the work, and how busy it is tells you when the box is struggling. Past about 80% busy, most servers slow down and start dropping things. Put an alert on that, and the desk hears about trouble before anyone is stuck outside.

reply.prompt: Gwilherm can change the desk's screen before the next shift. What should he change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Lower the speed alert from 2 s to 1 s, so the dashboard warns the desk much sooner.
options.verdict: A slowness alarm for a fast failure
options.part2: Gwilherm set the speed alert to 1 s. We replayed last night in the sim: from 00:00 every refusal took 40 ms, so the average only fell, from 50 ms to 41 ms. The alert never came near 1 s. At 05:00 the report said 43 ms, the fastest night on record, with no alert, and 0 of 40 offices cleaned. On a normal night the busiest minute averages a few hundred ms, so it never rings then either.
options.senior: A tighter threshold on the wrong signal is still the wrong signal. Speed alerts catch failures that are slow: a register that hangs, a server that queues. A failure that answers at once makes the average faster, not slower, so no speed limit, however tight, can see it. Measure failures as their own signal, and the speed of failures apart from the speed of successes.

options.text: Log every badge check in full detail, so the guard can read what each door was told.
options.part2: Gwilherm turned on full detail. In the sim's replay the log held 584 detailed refusals, each with the register's full answer: payment required. Nobody read them in the night. No alert, 0 of 40 offices cleaned. At half past seven he found the cause in two minutes, which is the real gain: the next morning goes faster.
options.senior: Detailed logs are the right tool for working out why, after you know something is wrong. They are poor at telling you that something is wrong, because a person has to go and read them. Keep them, make them structured so they can be searched, and let metrics and alerts decide when someone should look.

options.text: Alert when the badge server's CPU passes 80%, so the desk knows when it is struggling.
options.part2: Gwilherm added a CPU alert at 80%. In the sim's replay the badge server was never busier than 6.4%: a refusal is less work than a yes. No alert, 0 of 40 offices cleaned. The server was not struggling at all; it was doing exactly what it was told.
options.senior: CPU is a cause, a reason things might go wrong, and only one of many. Tonight's failure used almost no CPU. Alerting on causes means many alarms that hurt nobody, and silence for causes you didn't think of. Alert on symptoms people feel, such as entries that fail, and keep cause measures like CPU on the dashboard to help find the why.

options.text: Show the error rate on the dashboard, and alert when a door's good entries hit zero.
options.part2: Gwilherm added two lines to the screen: the error rate, and good entries a minute for each group of doors, front and side. The new alert rings when a group's taps have let nobody in for 5 minutes running. In the sim's replay the side doors were tapped from 00:00 to 00:04 with no good entry, so the alert rang at 00:05. I walked round with visitor badges, checked against the building's own list, and had the crew in by 00:15. 184 refusals instead of 584, and 40 of 40 offices cleaned, the last cleaner out at 04:26. The night report still said 47 ms, the fastest on record. The average lied again. This time something else was watching.
options.senior: Watch what people feel: the share of requests that fail, and whether good results are still happening at all. Show the speed of yes and the speed of no apart, so fast failures can't hide in the average. Page a person on symptoms like zero good entries, and keep causes such as CPU for finding out why. Then the logs and a trace tell you the reason in minutes.

sim.title: Run the night at Larkhollow's security desk
sim.lede: You're Gwilherm, replaying last night from 22:00, one minute per tick. Staff tap the front door, 4 a minute before 00:00 and 1 a minute after, and the building's list answers yes in 50 ms. The 8 cleaners arrive one a minute from 00:00 and use the side doors; their badges ask Sheencroft's register: yes in 600 ms on a normal night, or payment required in 40 ms from 00:00 tonight. A refused cleaner taps again twice a minute and goes home at 00:40. Each cleaner who gets in cleans 5 offices, 50 minutes each. Pick the register, which signals the dashboard draws, the alert rule, a split of answer speed into yes and no, and full detail in the log. When an alert rings, Temperance lets waiting cleaners in with visitor badges 10 minutes later.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to 05:00 as built. 584 refusals, the night average 43 ms, the fastest night on record, no alert, 0 of 40 offices cleaned. Switch on the split: yes 50 ms, no 40 ms. Trace the latest side-door tap: the register step is 40 ms, payment required. Set the register to normal and run again: 137 ms, an ordinary night, 40 of 40 cleaned. Now try each reply. A 1 s speed alert: no alert. Full detail: 584 detailed lines, no alert. A CPU alert at 80%: the server never passes 6.4%. Good entries at zero for 5 minutes: the alert rings at 00:05, the crew is in at 00:15, 40 of 40 cleaned.

explain.oneLine: Nothing on the screen was wrong; it just measured the wrong things. From 00:00 every cleaner's tap was refused in 40 ms, faster than any yes, so the average answer time fell to the fastest night on record while the error rate, which nobody was showing, sat at 94%. Busy and fast looked like healthy, and the only signal that said otherwise was a log nobody reads at night.

steps.title: What each tap did.
steps.text: First the cleaner tapped a side door, and the reader sent the badge to the badge server. Then the server read the badge type, contractor, in under 1 ms. Then it asked Sheencroft's register whether the badge was working tonight, and waited. From 00:00 the register answered at once, "payment required", in 40 ms. Last, the server applied its rule: anything but yes keeps the door shut. Every step did its job. The rule to refuse when the answer isn't yes is the safe one (fail closed, as in The Breaker Box); the trouble is that nobody was told.

steps.title: Why the average fell.
steps.text: An average adds every answer's time and divides by the number of answers. It does not care whether the answer was yes or no. Before 00:00 every answer was a staff check at 50 ms. From 00:07 each minute had 16 refusals at 40 ms and one staff yes at 50 ms: (16 x 40 + 50) / 17 = 41 ms. Over 00:00 to 05:00, 300 staff answers and 584 refusals made 43 ms. A normal night, with 56 cleaner taps at 600 ms, averages 137 ms. Google's engineers warn about exactly this: a fast error can drag the latency down and hide that requests are failing.

steps.title: Metrics: numbers over time.
steps.text: A metric is one number measured again and again: taps a minute, average answer time, CPU. Metrics are cheap to keep and easy to draw and alert on, which is why dashboards are made of them. What can go wrong: a metric only answers the question it was built for. The screen asked how busy and how fast. It never asked how many taps failed, so it could not say.

steps.title: Logs and traces: what happened, and where.
steps.text: A log is one line per event, written as it happens: here, every tap and what the register said. It held the whole story, 584 lines of payment required, and it told nobody, because a log waits to be read. A trace follows one request through every machine it touches and times each step. Gwilherm's trace showed the badge server under 1 ms and the register 40 ms, payment required: the cause in one picture. Logs and traces answer why; they rarely tell you when to look. That is the job of metrics and alerts (and of reading logs well, as in Logs at 3 AM).

steps.title: The four golden signals, and what should wake someone.
steps.text: Google's site reliability book suggests four signals for any service: latency (how long answers take), traffic (how many requests), errors (how many fail) and saturation (how full the machine is). Larkhollow's screen had two: traffic and latency, and its latency mixed yes and no together. Add errors as a rate, split latency into the speed of yes and the speed of no, and keep CPU as the saturation signal. Then decide what pages a person, meaning what sends an alert to someone's phone: a symptom people feel, such as a door group whose taps have let nobody in for 5 minutes. What can go wrong: an alert on a quiet door could ring for one person with an expired badge, so the rule needs taps in every one of the 5 minutes.

diagram.aria: The fix, with the three tools. A tap goes from the side doors to the badge server, which asks Sheencroft's register; tonight the register answers payment required in 40 ms. The badge server writes a log line for every tap, sends numbers to the dashboard, and keeps a trace of each tap whose register step shows 40 ms. The dashboard now shows taps, the speed of yes and of no, the error rate and good entries. Its alert rings when a door group's good entries stay at zero for 5 minutes, and calls the guard's desk, who lets the crew in by 00:15.

nodes.label: Dashboard
nodes.sub: taps, speed of yes and no

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next shift. The badge server writes a log line for every tap, sends numbers to the dashboard and keeps traces. The dashboard adds the error rate, good entries and the speed of yes and no apart, and an alert rings when a door group's good entries stay at zero for 5 minutes. In the sim's replay of last night: alert at 00:05, crew in at 00:15, 40 of 40 offices cleaned.

fix.title: The fix: show the failures, split the speed, and alert on what people feel
fix.text: Add an error-rate line to the dashboard: refused taps divided by all taps, each minute. Add good entries a minute for each door group, front and side. Split the answer speed into the speed of yes and the speed of no, so a fast refusal can't pull the yes line down. Keep traffic, and keep CPU as the saturation line, for finding causes. Then one alert that pages the desk: a door group whose taps have let nobody in for 5 minutes running. Keep the log, structured so it can be searched, and keep traces of each tap, for the why. In the sim's replay: the alert rings at 00:05, the crew is in by 00:15, 184 refusals instead of 584, and 40 of 40 offices cleaned.

limits: Good entries at zero only catches total failure. If the register refused half the crew, the side doors would still have good entries; the error rate line shows it, and a second alert on a high error rate for longer, say most taps failing for 15 minutes, covers it.

A wrong yes is invisible to every one of these signals. If the register let in someone it shouldn't, the error rate would read 0%. Only a check from outside, such as a test badge that must be refused, tapped on a schedule, can see a wrong answer.
An alert is only as good as the person it reaches. On a quiet night one alert at 00:05 is a gift; an alert that rings for every expired badge teaches the desk to ignore it.

rows: Simple; fine while errors are rare.
584 refusals, no alert, 0 of 40 cleaned; the report says fastest on record.
Catches a register that hangs sooner.
Fast refusals never trip it: no alert, 0 of 40 cleaned.
The cause is found in minutes next morning.
Nobody reads it at night: 584 detailed lines, 0 of 40 cleaned.
A cause, not a symptom: CPU peaks at 6.4%, no alert.
Error rate, speed split, good entries alert
Alert at 00:05, crew in by 00:15, 40 of 40 cleaned.
Misses partial failures and wrong yeses; the average still says 47 ms.

explain.seniorTake: Observability is being able to ask your system what it is doing and get a true answer. Use the three tools for what each does best: metrics to notice, numbers over time that are cheap to keep and to alert on; logs to explain, a line for each event with its details; traces to locate, one request's path with every step timed. Build the dashboard around the four golden signals, and never let one number stand for two kinds of request: show the speed of successes and of failures apart, and count failures as their own rate. Page people on symptoms users feel, such as nobody getting in, not on causes such as CPU, which belong on the screen for the investigation. And remember the one thing all of these miss: a wrong answer that looks like a right one, which only a test from outside can catch.

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: the four golden signals
realWorld.text: In "Monitoring Distributed Systems" (written by Rob Ewaschuk, edited by Betsy Beyer), Google writes: "The four golden signals of monitoring are latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. If you can only measure four metrics of your user-facing system, focus on these four." And: "If you measure all four golden signals and page a human when one signal is problematic (or, in the case of saturation, nearly problematic), your service will be at least decently covered by monitoring."

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: the latency of failures
realWorld.text: "It's important to distinguish between the latency of successful requests and the latency of failed requests. For example, an HTTP 500 error triggered due to loss of connection to a database or other critical backend might be served very quickly; however, as an HTTP 500 error indicates a failed request, factoring 500s into your overall latency might result in misleading calculations." It adds that "a slow error is even worse than a fast error", so "it's important to track error latency, as opposed to just filtering out errors." Larkhollow's 43 ms night is that misleading calculation.

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: symptoms and causes
realWorld.text: "Your monitoring system should address two questions: what's broken, and why? The "what's broken" indicates the symptom; the "why" indicates a (possibly intermediate) cause." On paging: "Every page should be actionable", and "it's better to spend much more effort on catching symptoms than causes". The chapter's conclusion says it "focuses primarily on symptoms for paging, reserving cause-oriented heuristics to serve as aids to debugging problems."

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: averages and the tail
realWorld.text: The same chapter warns that "it's tempting to design a system based upon the mean of some quantity", and gives an example: "If you run a web service with an average latency of 100 ms at 1,000 requests per second, 1% of requests might easily take 5 seconds." An average hides the slow end as easily as it hides fast failures.

realWorld.title: OpenTelemetry: signals
realWorld.text: OpenTelemetry, a free, shared set of rules and tools for collecting this data, calls the kinds of data a program gives out its signals, and its documentation lists traces, metrics and logs among them.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 CC7.2: monitoring for anomalies
realWorld.text: SOC 2's common criterion CC7.2 reads: "The entity monitors system components and the operation of those components for anomalies that are indicative of malicious acts, natural disasters, and errors affecting the entity's ability to meet its objectives; anomalies are analyzed to determine whether they represent security events." A door system refusing every contractor for five hours unseen is the kind of anomaly it means.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, A.8.15 and A.8.16
realWorld.text: Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 has a control titled Logging (A.8.15) and one titled Monitoring activities (A.8.16). The control wording is in the standard itself; the linked pages are secondary guides that name and explain them.

asked: Logs, metrics and traces: what is each for?
What are the four golden signals?
What should page someone at night?
interview.answer: Metrics are numbers measured over time, such as requests per second, error rate or latency percentiles. They're cheap to store and aggregate, so they drive dashboards and alerts: they tell you that something is wrong. Logs are records of individual events with their details, ideally structured with fields such as a request id, so you can search and filter them: they tell you what happened and why. Traces follow one request across services as a tree of timed steps, called spans: they tell you where the time went or where it failed. In practice you notice with metrics, locate with traces and explain with logs, and you link them with a shared request id. The four golden signals, from Google's SRE book, are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Two refinements matter: measure the latency of successful and failed requests separately, because fast errors pull the average down and hide failures, and look at percentiles like p99 rather than the mean. What should page someone is a symptom users feel that needs a human now: success rate collapsing, a key flow producing no good results, latency far beyond what users accept. Causes such as high CPU or a full queue belong on dashboards and in tickets, because they often hurt nobody and miss the failures you didn't predict. Every page should be actionable. A story I'd tell: an office building's badge system showed traffic and average answer time. A partner's register started refusing every cleaner in 40 ms instead of approving in 600 ms; the average fell, the dashboard called it the fastest night on record, and no office was cleaned. The fix was an error-rate signal, latency split by result, and an alert when a door group's successful entries stayed at zero for 5 minutes.

A free account that runs for a set time, then stops until someone pays. Larkhollow's three-month trial with the register ended at 00:00.
What the register answered to every check once the trial ended. The badge server treats anything but yes as no, so the door stayed shut.
When a check can't give a clear yes, refuse. Right for a door; it only hurts when nobody notices (The Breaker Box).
A screen of numbers about a system, each drawn as a line over time, like a car's dials for a building.
One number measured again and again over time, such as taps a minute or average answer time. Cheap to keep, easy to draw and alert on.

Larkhollow's only alert as built: it rings if the average answer time stays above 2 s for 5 minutes.
A program's diary: one line for each thing it does, written as it happens, with the time first (Logs at 3 AM).
The path of one request through every machine it touches, with each step timed. Gwilherm's showed the register step at 40 ms.
One timed step inside a trace, such as the badge server's check or the call to the register.
How well you can tell what a system is doing from what it reports about itself: its logs, metrics and traces.
One kind of information a system gives out for watching it, such as a metric, a log or a trace, or one line on a dashboard.
Google's four things to watch on any service: latency, traffic, errors and saturation.
How long an answer takes. Measure it for successes and failures apart: a fast failure makes the average look better.
How many requests come in, such as taps a minute. Last night it rose from 1 to 17 a minute as cleaners tapped again.
Requests that fail. At Larkhollow, refused taps.
Failed requests as a share of all requests. From 00:07 to 00:39 it was 16 of 17 taps a minute, 94%.
How full a machine is, such as how busy its CPU is. Most systems slow down before they are 100% full.
A computer's processor, the chip that does the work. How busy it is, as a percentage, is a common saturation signal.
What people feel when something breaks, such as a door that won't open. Good to page on.
Why something broke, such as a full CPU or an ended trial. Useful for finding out why, but there are too many possible causes to page on them all.
To send an alert to someone's phone so a person acts now, often at night. Every page should need a person to do something.
The dashboard's summary at 05:00 of the average answer time from 00:00. Last night: 43 ms, fastest on record.
Another word for the average.
The value a given share of answers come in under. p99 is the time 99 in 100 answers beat; it shows the slow end an average hides.
A log whose lines are labelled fields, such as door, badge type and register answer, so tools can search them exactly (Logs at 3 AM).
A short tag stuck on one request and passed along, so every machine's log lines and trace steps for it can be lined up (Logs at 3 AM).
A badge kept only for checking, such as one that must always be refused, tapped on a schedule to prove the checks still say no.
Checking a system from outside, as a user would, without looking at its insides. The only way to catch a wrong answer that looks right.
The list of who is working which shift. Sheencroft's rota says which cleaners should be in tonight.
Site reliability engineering: Google's name for engineers who keep large systems running, and the title of a book Google published about it.
A free, shared set of rules and tools for collecting logs, metrics and traces from programs, whatever tool later stores them.
The web's numbered answer for a request that failed inside the server. The SRE book uses it as its example of a fast error.
Another service your service calls and relies on, such as Sheencroft's register for the badge server. When it fails, yours fails too unless you planned for it.
An address on a server that answers with its current metrics, so a monitoring tool can collect them every few seconds.
A hands-on project session that unlocks after certain cases. G8 unlocks after this case.
A practice interview on the site. "Metrics and monitoring system" is a bonus one that sits after this case.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria.
A SOC 2 criterion: the company monitors its systems for anomalies that point to attacks, disasters or errors, and checks whether they are security events.

atWork: Look for a service whose dashboard shows traffic and average latency but no error rate. It is a common pattern: a dependency starts rejecting every request at once, failures come back faster than successes, the average latency drops, traffic climbs as clients retry, and the dashboard looks healthier than ever while users get nothing. Check three things. Is the error rate on the dashboard, per endpoint or per dependency? Is latency split by success and failure, and shown as percentiles, not only the mean? And does any alert fire on a symptom users feel, such as successful requests falling to zero, rather than only on CPU or slowness? Build Night G8 (unlocks after this case) has you add a metrics endpoint, structured logs with request ids, and a dashboard of rate, errors and latency for each backend. The bonus 3 AM Interview, Metrics and monitoring system, sits after this case. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, controls A.8.15 (Logging) and A.8.16 (Monitoring activities) apply, and if it is pursuing SOC 2, CC7.2 expects system components to be monitored for anomalies. Building error rates and symptom alerts in now saves rework at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your company's sign-in service has a dashboard of requests per second and average response time, with an alert if the average passes 1 s. One evening a change makes it reject every password in 5 ms. Requests double as people try again, the average response time goes down, and no alert rings. What happened, and what would you put on the dashboard and alert on?

keyIdeas.idea: The failures were fast, so they pulled the average down and hid that every request failed
Show the error rate, and the latency of successes and failures apart
Alert on the symptom users feel, such as successful sign-ins falling to zero, not on causes

recall.model: The failures were fast: rejecting a password in 5 ms is quicker than a real sign-in, so they pulled the average down and hid that every request was failing, and the retries doubled the traffic. A slowness alert can never see a fast error. I'd add the error rate to the dashboard, and show the latency of successful and failed requests separately, as percentiles. Then I'd alert on the symptom users feel: successful sign-ins per minute falling to zero, or the success rate dropping far below normal for a few minutes. CPU and other causes stay on the dashboard for working out why, and the logs and a trace of one rejected request would show which step said no.

recall.prompt: Which are Google's four golden signals?
recall.why: The SRE book's four are latency (how long answers take), traffic (how many requests), errors (how many fail) and saturation (how full the machine is). Larkhollow's screen showed only traffic and latency, with failures mixed into the latency.

recall.prompt: One request was slow, and it passed through three services. You want to see which step took the time. Which tool shows that best?
options: A metric of average answer time
A count of requests a minute
recall.why: A trace follows one request through every service and times each step, so the slow step stands out. Metrics tell you something is slow overall; logs tell you what each service did. Gwilherm's trace put the 40 ms on the register step.

recall.prompt: Which of these should wake someone at night?
options: No good entries at a door for 5 minutes while people keep tapping
recall.why: Page on symptoms people feel that need a person now. Nobody getting in while people are trying is exactly that. High CPU, a part-full disk and one refusal are worth seeing on a dashboard, but they often hurt nobody.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The error-rate line and the good-entries alert have worked all spring; in March the alert caught a broken reader on the west side door within 5 minutes. But last night at 02:14 the west side door let in a cleaner who left Sheencroft in April. She cleaned office 31 and was gone by 03:05. Sheencroft's register had started saying yes to every badge after an update on their side. Error rate: 0%. Good entries: normal. Answer speed: normal. No alert. We only know because Gwilherm checked the camera when the office's owner asked who had moved her chair.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the new dashboard stay calm, and what would catch this next time?

keyIdeas.idea: A wrong yes looks like a success, so the error rate and good entries both read healthy
Tap a known test badge that must be refused on a schedule, a check from outside, and alert if it opens
Compare the night's entries against Sheencroft's rota of who should be working

coldCase.model: It's the same trap in a new coat: a wrong answer that looks like a success. The error rate counts refusals, and a wrong yes is not an error to the badge server, so every signal stayed healthy. Nothing measured whether the yes was right. Add a test badge, a known badge registered as left that must be refused, and have a small program ask the register about it every few minutes, the way a user would, from outside; if the register ever says yes, alert. That is black-box testing, and it is the only kind of check that can see a wrong answer. Then compare each night's side-door entries against Sheencroft's rota, and flag any badge that isn't on it.
